content: The WHO Prequalification of In Vitro Diagnostics Programme is conducted following a structured process. The final outcome of the prequalification assessment depends on several factors: 1. The results of the dossier assessment and the acceptance of a corrective action plan, if required. 2. The results of inspections and the acceptance of a corrective action plan, if required. 3. Meeting the minimum acceptance criteria during laboratory evaluations. WHO determines whether an application will be prioritized for prequalification assessment based on WHO prioritization criteria and programmatic suitability. It is essential to confirm whether the product is manufactured by the original manufacturer (not re-branded) and to identify the regulatory version of the product submitted. Products that have undergone stringent regulatory assessments by certain national authorities may qualify for an abbreviated WHO prequalification assessment. However, even in such cases, laboratory evaluations and shortened inspections leveraging previous findings are still required. A product dossier contains documentation and data demonstrating that the in vitro diagnostic (IVD) device complies with essential safety and performance principles. International best practices, such as those issued by the International Medical Device Regulators Forum (IMDRF) and other standards from ISO and CLSI, are considered during the review process. WHO evaluates the performance and use of IVDs specifically from the perspective of WHO Member States, focusing on aspects like stability, risk assessment, and instructions for use. Any non-conformities identified are rated, and manufacturers must submit a corrective action plan detailing how and when requirements will be met. The WHO inspection process for manufacturing sites involves several stages: Stage 1: Evaluation of readiness for inspection through a desktop review of quality documentation or a brief on-site inspection. Stage 2: A full on-site inspection to assess the implementation of the quality management system, facilities, warehousing, staff competence, critical suppliers, internal audits, and management commitment. Dossier assessors may attend to confirm dossier aspects. Follow-up: Confirmation of the implementation of corrective actions from Stage 2, which may or may not require another on-site inspection. Surveillance: Risk-based, with at least annual reporting required. Re-inspection: Risk-based, conducted every 3–5 years for WHO prequalified products. All inspected sites must meet prequalification requirements, demonstrating a fully implemented quality management system, risk management per ISO 14971, product stability, routine manufacturing, and sufficient capacity for reliable delivery. WHO laboratory evaluations are comparative, testing each assay on the same globally sourced clinical specimen reference panel and commercially acquired panels for seroconversion and low antibody/antigen titers. These evaluations assess technical and performance characteristics, such as sensitivity, specificity, and seroconversion sensitivity, relative to other similar assays. Manufacturers send one or two production lots to WHO Collaborating Centres or designated laboratories for evaluation. WHO issues a technical report on performance and operational characteristics and determines if the assay meets prequalification requirements. Minimum acceptable performance criteria for serology assays include: Sensitivity: >99% for RDTs, 100% for EIAs. Specificity: >98% for both RDTs and EIAs. Inter-reader variability: <5% for RDTs. Invalid rate: <5% for both RDTs and EIAs. Operational characteristics for RDTs and EIAs are also evaluated, including items required but not provided with test kits, time to first result, throughput per operator, storage stability, in-use stability, and the number of steps required for the test procedure. Once a prequalification decision is made, WHO issues a public report, and the product is added to the list of WHO prequalified products, making it eligible for WHO and UN procurement. Post-prequalification, manufacturers must conduct post-market activities to ensure the continued quality, safety, and performance of the IVD. They must notify WHO of any changes to the product or quality management system for evaluation. The IMDRF is working towards harmonizing national regulatory standards for medical devices, including IVDs, to increase efficiency for both reviewers and manufacturers. Post-market surveillance ensures the ongoing safety and performance of IVDs after market release. Manufacturers must monitor events affecting assay quality, safety, or performance, evaluate residual risks, and implement risk mitigation measures as needed. WHO collects post-market data, including preand post-distribution lot verification testing results, complaints, and evaluation data, to coordinate actions and ensure traceability. Quality control (QC) for HIV rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) involves monitoring the analytical performance of the assay. External QC specimens, such as low-reactive biological specimens, can be used to challenge assay performance. These specimens are typically prepared by diluting strongly reactive HIV-positive specimens in a suitable matrix. QC results should be recorded, analyzed, and monitored for trends requiring management. QC specimens should be run weekly, for new operators, new test kit lots, new shipments, or when environmental conditions deviate from recommended ranges. WHO is developing specific guidance on preparing QC specimens for RDTs.
